lines: Routine health maintenance examination with review of hormone replacement therapy started three years ago

She reports being generally healthy and maintains a fairly active lifestyle.
Approximately three years ago, she began experiencing bothersome hot flashes, night sweats, and difficulty sleeping due to vasomotor instability.
At the time, her physician prescribed hormone replacement therapy, consisting of estrogen combined with progestin, which she continues to take daily.
She reports that her menopausal symptoms have greatly improved since starting therapy, and she feels much more comfortable in daily life.
She denies vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, bloating, or urinary symptoms.
She has not experienced breast pain, nipple discharge, or palpable breast lumps.

She explains that her personal life has been complicated recently.
Her father became ill last year, and she moved in with him to help take care of him.
She describes long days of cooking, cleaning, and organizing medications for her father, which made her feel both exhausted and emotionally fulfilled.

Recently, her father decided to move across the state to take advantage of a better insurance policy, which has left her with mixed emotions—she misses him but is relieved to have more time for her own life again.
Outside of her family responsibilities, she is passionate about rare plants.
She has collected exotic species from dozens of different countries.
She describes trips to South America to find rare orchids, journeys to Southeast Asia for tropical ferns, and exhibitions in Europe where she has displayed parts of her collection.
During her travels, she often met friends in small taverns where they would exchange plants and stories of botany.
She proudly states that she has cultivated her greenhouse into a museum of biodiversity, with species rarely seen outside their native ecosystems.
Despite her vibrant hobbies, she now finds herself struggling to maintain the energy to care for her plants.
She reports being winded when watering or repotting.
She does not smoke, drink, or use recreational drugs.
She has never smoked and has no known environmental exposures to asbestos, silica, or coal dust.

She denies fevers, chills, or weight loss, but says her appetite has been slightly reduced because “food just doesn’t taste good when you can’t catch your breath.” She has no chest pain, orthopnea, or leg swelling.
Vital signs reveal an oxygen saturation of 91% on room air, respiratory rate of 21/min, and blood pressure of 122/74 mm Hg.
Her temperature is normal.
On physical examination, she is in mild respiratory distress at rest.
Cardiac examination shows a regular rate and rhythm without murmurs.
Pulmonary examination reveals bilateral end-inspiratory crackles most pronounced at the lung bases.
There is no wheezing or rhonchi.
Clubbing of the fingers is noted.
The remainder of the exam, including joint inspection, reveals only mild deformities consistent with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis but no acute synovitis.
Chest radiography demonstrates diffuse interstitial opacities.
High-resolution CT of the chest reveals a reticular pattern with areas of honeycombing.
Pulmonary function testing demonstrates a restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity and a decreased diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO).
